results.summary: The class of elementary amenable groups is the smallest class of groups that contains every finite group and every abelian group and is closed under isomorphisms, subgroups, quotients, extensions and directed unions. results.title: Kourovka Problem 16.52 (Linnell–Schick)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that every finitely presented elementary amenable group $G$ is solvable-by-finite, that is, $G$ has a solvable subgroup of finite index.

results.title: Finitely presented elementary amenable groups need not be virtually solvable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a finitely presented elementary amenable group $G$ that is not solvable-by-finite: no subgroup of finite index in $G$ is solvable. This answers Kourovka Problem 16.52 (P. Linnell, T. Schick) in the negative.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 16.75: one-relator automorphism groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The proposition that there exist a natural number $n$ and an element $r$ of the free group on generators $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ such that the one-relator group $\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid r \rangle$ is non-abelian and is isomorphic to the automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(H)$ of some group $H$. The problem is due to M. V. Neshchadim.

results.title: Some non-abelian one-relator group is an automorphism group
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There exist a natural number $n$ and an element $r$ of the free group on generators $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ such that the one-relator group $\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid r \rangle$ is non-abelian and is isomorphic to the automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(H)$ of some group $H$. This answers Kourovka Problem 16.75 in the affirmative.

results.title: Ducci coefficients
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$, $r$ and $s$, the Ducci coefficient is $a_{r,s} = \sum_{0 \le j \le r,\ j \equiv s - 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)} \binom{r}{j}$, where $s - 1$ is read as $0$ when $s = 0$ and congruence modulo $0$ is equality.

results.title: Binomial coefficients $\binom{p^k - 1}{j}$ modulo $p$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime, let $k \ge 1$, and let $j$ be an integer with $0 \le j \le p^k - 1$. Then $\binom{p^k - 1}{j} \equiv (-1)^j \pmod{p}$.

results.title: Binomial coefficients $\binom{p^k - p^{k-1}}{j}$ modulo $p$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $k \ge 2$, and let $j$ be an integer with $0 \le j \le p^k - p^{k-1}$. If $j = c\,p^{k-1}$ for an integer $c$, then $\binom{p^k - p^{k-1}}{j} \equiv (-1)^c \pmod{p}$; otherwise $\binom{p^k - p^{k-1}}{j} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$.

results.title: Reduction of Ducci coefficients modulo $p$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For integers $N \ge 1$, $r \ge 0$ and $s \ge 1$ write $a^{(N)}_{r,s} = \sum_{0 \le j \le r,\ j \equiv s - 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ N)} \binom{r}{j}$ for the Ducci coefficients of length $N$. Let $p$ be a prime, let $k \ge 0$ and $n_1 \ge 2$ be integers, and let $n = p^k n_1$. Then for every integer $c \ge 1$ and every integer $b$ with $0 \le b < n_1$, $a^{(n)}_{c p^k,\, b p^k + 1} \equiv a^{(n_1)}_{c,\, b + 1} \pmod{p}$.

results.title: Ducci predecessor criterion for even length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m \ge 0$ be an integer, let $n \ge 2$ be even, and write $\mathbb{Z}_m = \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ (so $\mathbb{Z}_0 = \mathbb{Z}$). A tuple $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \mathbb{Z}_m^n$ has a Ducci predecessor, that is, a tuple $y \in \mathbb{Z}_m^n$ with $y_i + y_{i+1} = x_i$ for all $i$ (indices taken cyclically, so $y_{n+1} = y_1$), if and only if $x_1 - x_2 + x_3 - \cdots + x_{n-1} - x_n = 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_m$.

results.title: Evaluation of divisors as a group homomorphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a commutative group $G$ and a function $f : C \to G$, this is the monoid homomorphism from the group of divisors on $C$, written multiplicatively, to $G$ that sends a divisor $D$ to the finite product $\prod_{P \in \operatorname{supp} D} f(P)^{D(P)}$.

results.title: Evaluation of a divisor against a function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a commutative group $G$, a function $f : C \to G$ and a divisor $D$ on $C$, the evaluation of $D$ against $f$ is the element $f(D) = \prod_{P \in \operatorname{supp} D} f(P)^{D(P)}$ of $G$.

results.title: Evaluation is a product over the support
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a commutative group $G$, every function $f : C \to G$ and every divisor $D$ on $C$, the evaluation of $D$ against $f$ equals $\prod_{P \in \operatorname{supp} D} f(P)^{D(P)}$, the product over the points in the support of $D$.

results.title: The zero divisor evaluates to one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a commutative group $G$ and every function $f : C \to G$, the evaluation of the zero divisor on $C$ against $f$ is the identity element $1$ of $G$.

results.title: Evaluation of a one-point divisor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a commutative group $G$, every function $f : C \to G$, every point $P \in C$ and every integer $n$, the divisor $n \cdot P$, with coefficient $n$ at $P$ and $0$ elsewhere, evaluates against $f$ to $f(P)^n$.

results.title: Evaluation is multiplicative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a commutative group $G$, every function $f : C \to G$ and all divisors $D_1, D_2$ on $C$, writing $f(D)$ for the evaluation of a divisor $D$ against $f$, we have $f(D_1 + D_2) = f(D_1) \, f(D_2)$.

results.title: Evaluation of an integer multiple
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a commutative group $G$, every function $f : C \to G$, every integer $n$ and every divisor $D$ on $C$, writing $f(D)$ for the evaluation of $D$ against $f$, we have $f(nD) = f(D)^n$.

results.title: Smooth Poincaré conjecture in dimension 3
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a nonempty, compact, simply connected Hausdorff space with a smooth ($C^\infty$) manifold structure modelled on $\mathbb{R}^3$, without boundary. Then $M$ is $C^\infty$-diffeomorphic to the unit sphere $S^3 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^4 : \|x\| = 1\}$ with its standard smooth structure.

results.title: Topological Poincaré conjecture in dimension 3
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Topological Poincaré conjecture in dimension 4
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Hausdorff space with an atlas of charts to $\mathbb{R}^4$ (a topological 4-manifold without boundary, not assumed second countable). If $M$ is homotopy equivalent to the unit sphere $S^4 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^5 : \|x\| = 1\}$, then $M$ is homeomorphic to $S^4$.

results.title: Topological Poincaré conjecture in dimensions at least 5
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 5$ and let $M$ be a Hausdorff space with an atlas of charts to $\mathbb{R}^n$ (a topological $n$-manifold without boundary, not assumed second countable). If $M$ is homotopy equivalent to the unit sphere $S^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} : \|x\| = 1\}$, then $M$ is homeomorphic to $S^n$.

results.title: $(0,2)$-graphs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is a $(0,2)$-graph when every two distinct vertices of $G$ have either exactly zero or exactly two common neighbors.

results.title: The three-chromatic $(0,2)$-graph conjecture
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: It asserts that there are a natural number $n$ and a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every two distinct vertices have either zero or two common neighbors, such that the chromatic number of $G$ is $3$.

results.title: No finite $(0,2)$-graph has chromatic number three
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every simple graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every two distinct vertices have either zero or two common neighbors, the chromatic number of $G$ is not $3$. In particular, the three-chromatic $(0,2)$-graph conjecture is false.

results.title: Odd cycle transversal instances
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An odd cycle transversal instance is a triple $(n, es, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the bound on the number of removed vertices).

results.title: Graph of an odd cycle transversal instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an odd cycle transversal instance $(n, es, K)$, its graph is the graph of the edge list $es$ on $n$ vertices: the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $es$.

results.title: Well-formed odd cycle transversal instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An odd cycle transversal instance $(n, es, K)$ is well formed when the list $es$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $es$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and $(v, u)$ does not belong to $es$.

results.title: Feasible odd cycle transversal instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An odd cycle transversal instance $(n, es, K)$ is feasible when there is a set $S$ of at most $K$ vertices of its graph such that the subgraph induced on the vertices outside $S$ is bipartite.

results.title: ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an odd cycle transversal instance $(n, es, K)$ that is well formed and feasible. Well formed means that $es$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $es$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin es$; feasible means that some set of at most $K$ vertices…

results.title: ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL, which accepts a bitstring exactly when it decodes to a well-formed instance $(n, es, K)$ whose graph becomes bipartite after removing some set of at most $K$ vertices, belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.
